# Georgia Senate candidate reports $50M self-loan; FEC issues warning letter

- By [Joedy McCreary](https://www.opensecrets.org/news/author/jmccreary/)
- [May 15, 2026 3:14 pm](https://www.opensecrets.org/news/2026/05/)

- [Share this article on Twitter](https://twitter.com/share?url=http://www.opensecrets.org/news/2026/05/georgia-senate-candidate-christina-clement-reports-50m-self-loan)

(Photo from campaign website) A write%E2%80%91in%E2%80%A6 %0D%0A%0D%0Ahttp://www.opensecrets.org/news/2026/05/georgia-senate-candidate-christina-clement-reports-50m-self-loan)

Embed

![Georgia Senate Christina Clement](https://cdn1.opensecrets.org/news/wp-content/uploads/2026/05/15150322/imageedit_12_2046661310.jpg)

_Christina Clement, a candidate for Senate in Georgia, reporting loan her campaign $50 million. (Photo from campaign website)_

A write‑in Senate candidate in Georgia who reported loaning her own campaign more than $50 million has drawn a warning letter from the Federal Election Commission saying the filing may be inaccurate and reminding her that knowingly submitting false information can carry civil or criminal penalties.

In its [most recent quarterly filing](https://www.documentcloud.org/documents/28124612-clement-q1/), Christina Clement’s campaign stated that she loaned it nearly $50.3 million – a staggering sum 10 times greater than any other self-loan listed [in the FEC database](https://www.fec.gov/data/receipts/?data_type=processed&two_year_transaction_period=2026&min_date=01%2F01%2F2025&max_date=12%2F31%2F2026&line_number=F3-13A) for the current election cycle. The agency responded with [an April 28 letter](https://www.documentcloud.org/documents/28124610-fec-clement/) saying the report may not be “true, correct or complete” and reminding her that she could face fines or referral for false filing.

The FEC on Friday then removed the loan entry from its searchable online database and placed it in [a separate repository for miscellaneous documents on the committee’s page](https://www.fec.gov/data/committee/C00857128/?cycle=2026&tab=filings#other), agency spokesperson Myles Martin said.

Clement said the filing reflects a complex valuation of a license to her own currency-related intellectual property and referred OpenSecrets to a [website describing the “LND”](https://stateoflocnation.com/soln-central-bank-gov) monetary unit, but did not provide evidence that any funds were deposited into the campaign’s account. In its May 5 [response to the FEC](https://docquery.fec.gov/pdf/446/202605059866811446/202605059866811446.pdf), Clement’s campaign said the committee assigned a fair market value to the license that “reflects the scope of use, supporting research and the overall body of work associated with the intellectual property.”

The letter surfaced as OpenSecrets examined self‑funding patterns in the four years since the [Supreme Court struck down](https://apnews.com/article/us-supreme-court-elections-campaigns-government-and-politics-ted-cruz-a4905abe71982ec1fef0e5c7ef183b95) a provision limiting how much of a candidate’s personal loan could be repaid with money raised after Election Day. In [FEC v. Ted Cruz for Senate](https://www.supremecourt.gov/opinions/21pdf/21-12_m6hn.pdf) – decided May 16, 2022 – the court’s conservative majority eliminated the $250,000 cap on post-election loan repayment, a change experts say has encouraged larger and more frequent self‑loans.

In response to an OpenSecrets inquiry, Martin pointed to the [agency’s internal procedures](https://www.fec.gov/resources/cms-content/documents/Final-Redacted-2025-2026-RAD-Review-Referral-Procedures.pdf#page=169) for reviewing “potentially inflated receipts” by self‑funding candidates, a category that includes unusually large or implausible loans. He also noted that, as part of that process, filings deemed unverified or potentially false are moved to the commission’s “False and Fictitious Filings” section, where they remain public but are excluded from its searchable database and campaign finance statistics as a way of maintaining the accuracy of the FEC’s verified records. And while the agency has [lacked a quorum of commissioners](https://www.opensecrets.org/news/2025/05/democratic-report-calls-fec-a-broken-agency-on-its-50th-anniversary/) for more than a year, Martin said that has no effect on this type of review because the procedures were approved when it did have one.

While FEC records show Clement [is a Republican](https://www.fec.gov/data/candidate/S6GA00366/?cycle=2026&election_full=false), her name [does not appear on the ballot](https://www.fultoncountyga.gov/-/media/2026-Election/May-19-Election/2026-05-May-19-General-Primary-REPUBLICAN-composite-ballot-vFINAL-2.pdf) for the [May 19 Georgia primary](https://www.savannahnow.com/story/news/local/2026/04/02/georgia-republican-senate-primary-candidates-speak-at-savannah-area-event/89423953007/). Clement describes herself as the [leader of the State of Loc Nation](https://img1.wsimg.com/blobby/go/ce3e657e-cb91-4798-9eeb-a96d1f26df07/SOLN_Mutual_Engagement_Policy_Truth_and_Right%20.pdf), an “indigenous sovereign entity representing Afro-descended people and historically marginalized communities,” and [claimed to have access to $2 billion](https://stateoflocnation.com/f/dr-clement-officially-enters-2026-georgia-us-senate-with-2b) in funds when she announced her Senate bid in August 2025.

In its quarterly filing dated March 31, the campaign – the State of Loc Nation for Clement for Senate – reported $50,248,695.59 in cash on hand and an [unsecured loan from Clement totaling $50,250,000](https://web.archive.org/web/20260514183059/https://docquery.fec.gov/cgi-bin/forms/C00857128/1960374/sc/ALL). The loan was incurred Jan. 1 with a 0% interest rate and is due on demand. The FEC document – which uses a Delaware mailing address – also shows $930 in contributions and $2,234.41 in expenditures.

Clement’s response to OpenSecrets included a set of [self‑prepared notarized documents](https://archive.org/details/signed-lnd-ip-license-2026-ia-copy-1_202602/page/n5/mode/2up) asserting that the campaign’s reported $50.25 million “loan” reflects the value of a limited non‑exclusive license to her own intellectual property – a framework she calls “LND” and describes as “the official Black dollar.” The documents assign multimillion‑dollar values to various components of that IP and characterize the total as a candidate loan under federal regulations. But they do not include any evidence showing that $50 million was ever deposited into the campaign’s account. Nor do they demonstrate the existence of liquid funds corresponding to the amount reported to the FEC. Clement’s reference to the website came in response to a follow-up email from OpenSecrets asking whether the reported loan amount was deposited into the campaign’s account.

The campaign’s response to the FEC also included an acknowledgement of an additional $900 in previously unreported itemized contributions received in March.

John Martin, an election law scholar and assistant professor of law at Quinnipiac University who has [studied](https://lawreview.law.pitt.edu/ojs/lawreview/article/view/1098/708) candidate self-loans, identified two plausible explanations for Clement’s filing: It’s a typo, or it’s fabricated.

“I don’t know Ms. Clement’s motives, but I would say in an era where someone can use third-party contributions to pay off their self-loans – and attached interest – I wouldn’t be surprised if somebody forged a self-loan to profit off third-party contributions,” Martin said in an email to OpenSecrets. “Unfortunately, the process for reporting something like this to the FEC is not simple – since you need to notarize your complaint – so a candidate could potentially get away with such a scheme.”

The FEC’s letter states that Clement “may have failed to include the true, correct or complete itemization of receipts and/or disbursements” on the filing. It also notes that the commission may report apparent violations to law enforcement and that the signer of the form – Clement, also listed as the group’s treasurer – [may face](https://www.fec.gov/resources/cms-content/documents/Final-Redacted-2025-2026-RAD-Review-Referral-Procedures.pdf#page=170) [civil penalties](https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=(title:52%20section:30109%20edition:prelim)) and [referral](https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=(title:52%20section:30107%20edition:prelim)) if it determines she knowingly filed false information.

The amount of Clement’s reported loan dwarfs all others in the FEC database: Six self-loans of $5 million were listed, including two by former Rep. David Trone (D-Md.) to his campaign, [David Trone for Maryland Inc.](https://www.opensecrets.org/profiles/david-trone/us_congress/summary?mpid=1113610) Trone, who founded the Total Wine & More chain of superstores before becoming the [top self-funding candidate in the 2024 cycle](https://www.opensecrets.org/elections-overview/top-self-funders?cycle=2024), spent more than $62 million of his own money that year in his [failed Senate bid](https://www.opensecrets.org/news/2024/05/self-funded-candidates-put-166-million-in-campaigns/), according to OpenSecrets data. [FEC records show](https://www.fec.gov/data/receipts/?data_type=processed&contributor_name=trone&two_year_transaction_period=2024&min_date=01%2F01%2F2023&max_date=12%2F31%2F2024&line_number=F3-13A) he made 31 self-loans before that year’s primary totaling more than $62 million.
